atha aṣṭamo vimarśaḥ | pūrvaṃ yadanuttaramamṛtabhūmimāsādya saptamīṃ kalanām | viśrāmyati tatpraṇamāmyamṛtāṅgadaṃ parānandi || evaṃ jñānasmṛtyapohanaśaktimāneko'ntaḥkṛtānantaviśvarūpaḥ, - itīyat vitatya upapāditam | adhunā maheśvara iti nirṇetavyam | tatra māheśvaryaṃ jñānaviṣayaṃ kriyāviṣayaṃ ca, ādyamatraiva jñānādhikāre nirṇīyate | evaṃ jñātā prakṛtitaḥ pratyayataśca nirṇīto bhavati | tatra jñānaṃ nāma saṃvedanamahamiti yat, tadeva svayaṃbheditābhāsoparāgarūṣaṇāsaṅkucitamucyate | tataśca ābhāsavarge yat svātantryaṃ, tadeva jñānaviṣayaṃ māheśvaraṃ nirṇetuṃ tātkālikākṣa.......................................... | ityādinā ......................... śuddhe jñānakriye yataḥ | ityantena ślokaikādaśakena vimarśāntaramārabhyate | tatra ābhāsāntaramābhāso'pekṣate kaścit, kaścit na tathā,- iti ślokena uktvā, tathāpi sa eka eva ābhāsa iti ślokāntareṇa ucyate, arthakriyābhāso'pi tathaiva ābhāsaniyata iti dvayena, kutra ābhāse sā arthakriyeti dvayena, ābhāsāntaravaicitrye bhittikalpamāntaratvamiti ślokena, bāhyatvaṃ svarūpato vibhāgataśca dvayena, jñānādiśaktyāśrayasya upasaṃhāraḥ ekena, maheśvaratvamupasaṃharatā bhāvikriyādhikāropakṣepa ekena,- iti tātparyam | atha pratisūtramarthanirūpaṇam | uktamidaṃ parameśvaraniṣṭha eva sarvo vyavahāra iti | tatra syādāśaṅkā- vyavahārasya anuprāṇaka eka eva, nahi tadatiriktaṃ vyavahārasya kimapi nijaṃ tattvamasti, tataśca sphuṭatvā- (page 408) sphuṭatvaprāyapracuravaicitryacarcāvicāre nimittaṃ na labhyate-iti | tāmapāsitumucyate tātkālikākṣasāmakṣyasāpekṣāḥ kevalaṃ kvacit | ābhāsā anyathānyatra tvandhāndhatamasādiṣu || 1 || vyavahāro bhagavati sarva iti satyamidam, tatra vaktavyāntaramucyate,- iti kevalapadam | tatkālabhavaṃ nikaṭavarti yadakṣasāmakṣyamaindriyakādi pratyakṣaṃ, tadapekṣamāṇāstatsaṃskārabalotthitā ghaṭo'yamityādyā ābhāsāḥ pratyakṣasamanantarabhāvini vikalpavyavahāre anyatra tu andhādivyavahāre anyathā iti na tātkālikamakṣasāmakṣyamapekṣante ciravṛttasaṃskārotthāpitāstadā te ābhāsā
**The great-Lordship: the freedom in the appearance-group** The knower, with his powers of knowledge, memory, and removal, the inner-made-infinite-world-form, has been established. Now Abhinavagupta asks what makes him *maheśvara*, the great Lord. The great-Lordship (māheśvarya) is twofold: it is directed at objects of knowledge and at objects of action. Here, in the jñānādhikāra, the knowledge-directed lordship is determined. What is the jñāna? It is the self-experience "aham" — the "I" — contracted by the tint of the self-splitting appearance. And the lordship is the *freedom in the appearance-group*: the freedom with which the appearances arise, vary, and depend on one another. The doubt arises at once. "All the dealing," the objector says, "is in the param-eśvara alone. But the dealing's animator is one — there is nothing of its own beyond it. So what cause is there for the varied dealing of the world, with all its clearness and variety?" And kārikā 1 answers: the appearances are not all alike. Some are dependent on the eye's co-presence at that time — the "this jar," raised by the impression's strength, depending on the perception that is near, sensory — and these appear in the construction-dealing that follows immediately upon the perception. Others appear otherwise — in the blind, in the darkness, and the rest, where there is no such eye-co-presence. The appearances are not a single flat mass; they have their own dependence, their own conditions, their own arising. And this is precisely the freedom. The varied dealing of the world is not caused by something outside the Lord; it is the Lord's own freedom in the appearance-group — the freedom by which some appearances depend on the senses, some do not, yet all are one. The appearance-group is not inert; it is the manifestation of the Lord's freedom, the jñāna as the "aham" that shines through all the appearances, unified in the one knower. So the aṣṭamo vimarśa opens the great-Lordship. The Lord is maheśvara because he is free in the appearance-group: the appearances arise, depend, and vary by his freedom, and yet they are one, because they are all his own "aham"-manifestation. The knowledge-directed lordship is this freedom — the self-experience that runs through all the appearances, the one "I" in which the whole world of appearances rests. And this, Abhinavagupta will go on to show, grounds both the knowledge and the action — the full great-Lordship of the one who is free in all the appearances, the maheśvara. ---

> The claim is that the essence of light is the reflexive awareness, not the bare showing of objects. > The crystal supplies the contrast: a light that merely showed the world without knowing that it showed > it would be no different from crystal — it would reflect, but be inert. What makes the light conscious > is the self-awareness in the very act of manifesting. The passage then identifies this self-knowing > with the supreme speech (parā-vāk) and with the Lord's freedom and lordship. > > The identification with the Word is the extension: the reflexivity is not a bare self-presence but > the supreme speech from which the lower levels of language descend. This is why the word-joined "I" > need not be a construction — language is the form the self-grasp takes, not something that produces > it. The passage establishes the reflexivity claim; the full account of the powers and the Lordship is > developed in the following vimarśas. parā-vāk (supreme speech) · svātantrya/aiśvarya (freedom/lordship).
